title: They Had Kings First — the List, the Chiefs, Edom
blocks: Brothers and sisters, peace to you. The chapter set in front of us today is the one a Bible-reading plan is most likely to skip straight over — Genesis chapter 36, the family register of Esau. Forty-three verses, one long string of names, reading like a page out of a household registration office.

But I would like you to hear one sentence first. Hidden inside this chapter is a verse that stings the eyes: "These are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom, before any king reigned over the children of Israel" (Genesis 36:31). And then, in one breath, Scripture lists eight kings.

Put it another way. By the time Esau's descendants had cities, had kings, had borders and a complete set of administrative records, Jacob's descendants were still nothing more than a crowd of people — and what lay immediately ahead of them was going down into Egypt to be slaves for four hundred years.
So the question this lesson puts to you is this: has there ever been a season when you looked around and saw that the people who pay God no attention seem to be doing rather better than you?
1. The Branch Set Aside — God Gives a Full Account of That One Too
Verse 1: "Now this is the history of the generations of Esau (that is, Edom)."

"Generations" in the original is תּוֹלְדוֹת (*toldot*). This is the skeleton word of Genesis; it occurs eleven times across the whole book, and every time it appears, a new section of the story is beginning.

And Genesis has a very fixed habit in the way it writes. At every turning point it first finishes off the account of the branch that is *not* the main line, and only then comes back to the main line. Ishmael's descendants are dealt with first (25:12–18), and only then does the text move on to Isaac; here Esau's descendants are dealt with in full, and only then, in chapter 37, does the story of Joseph begin.

Brothers and sisters, notice the heart behind that arrangement. God could have disposed of the whole business with a single line — "Esau also had descendants" — and moved on. Instead Scripture gives him forty-three verses: his three wives, his five sons, his eleven grandsons, the roll of the chiefs, eight kings, their capital cities, the borders of their land.
Even the one who was set aside — God remembers him, and remembers him down to the last detail.

And what moves me most is verse 24: "These are the children of Zibeon: Aiah and Anah. This is Anah who found the hot springs in the wilderness, as he fed the donkeys of Zibeon his father." A boy out in the wilderness pasturing his father's donkeys, walking along, and he comes upon a spring of water. How small a thing is that? And yet it was written into the Bible, and four thousand years later we are still reading it.
God's memory does not work the way ours does. We remember the great events. He remembers the people.

So if you feel today that you are the one who has been set aside — nobody remembers your name, nobody knows which patch of wilderness you are pasturing donkeys in — this chapter is for you. You are in his book.

Verses 6 to 8 tell us why Esau moved away: "Esau took his wives … and went into a land away from his brother Jacob. For their substance was too great for them to dwell together, and the land of their travels couldn't bear them because of their livestock."

"Couldn't bear them" in the original is לֹא יָכְלָה לָשֵׂאת, literally "the land could not carry them." That same sentence had already appeared, word for word, back in chapter 13, when Abram and Lot separated: "The land was not able to bear them, that they might live together."

And there is one more thing worth mentioning here. Verse 2 says that the wives Esau took were "from the daughters of Canaan." Chapter 26 puts it very bluntly: "They grieved Isaac's and Rebekah's spirits." And in chapter 28 Isaac gives Jacob one particular charge: "You shall not take a wife of the daughters of Canaan." This was the deepest fork in the road of Esau's whole life — not that bowl of red stew, but those marriages.

The place where a person really goes off course is very often not one impulsive decision. It is his choice of the people he will live his days alongside. That is something we have to weigh with great care — for our children, and for ourselves.

Only this time, the parting is a peaceful one. After that embrace in chapter 33, the two brothers never fell out again. Esau chose for himself to go south, to the hill country of Seir. "Away from" in the original is מִפְּנֵי, literally "from before the face of" his brother Jacob.
Being reconciled does not always mean living together. Some relationships are restored and still need distance. That is not a failure. That is wisdom.
A whole chapter of nothing but names — can a Bible-reading plan simply skip it?

You can skip it, but you will miss something very precious. Genesis has a fixed habit: at every turning point it first finishes off the branch that is not the main line, and then returns to the main line — Ishmael is dealt with first, and only then Isaac; Esau is dealt with in full, and only then, in chapter 37, does Joseph's story begin. God could have disposed of it with one line, "Esau also had descendants", and instead he gave him forty-three verses. So the real message of this chapter is not in the names; it is in the attitude: even the one who was set aside, God accounts for down to the last detail. If you feel today that you are the one nobody remembers, this chapter is precisely the one written for you.
That boy in verse 24 who came upon the hot springs — why is he worth writing into the Bible at all?

A boy out in the wilderness pasturing his father's donkeys, walking along, and he finds a spring of water — how small a thing is that? And yet it was written into the Bible, and four thousand years later we are still reading it. That verse is like a marker God deliberately left behind, to remind us that his memory does not work the way ours does: we remember the great events, he remembers the people. This matters enormously to anyone who serves quietly. You wash the dishes in the kitchen, you direct the cars in the car park, you answer the messages in the group chat one by one, and nobody is going to remember any of it — but that does not mean it was never written down. God's book and the church's annual report are not keeping the same set of records.
2. A Light from the Original: "Chief" Forty Times, "He Died" Seven Times
There are two words in this chapter that recur so often it cannot possibly be an accident.

The first is "chief", in the original אַלּוּף (*aluf*), which properly means "the head of a thousand." That word appears more than forty times in this one chapter. Esau's descendants, one after another after another, are every last one of them a "chief."

The second word turns up in that roll of kings in verses 31 to 39. Eight kings, and every one of them is recorded by exactly the same formula: so-and-so reigned, the name of his city was such-and-such — and then, "so-and-so died."
"Died" in the original is וַיָּמָת (*vayamat*), and in that short passage it occurs seven times.

And look at the word that comes immediately after it: "so-and-so reigned in his place", in the original תַּחְתָּיו, literally "in his stead, in the place where he sat." Eight kings, eight replacements — and not one of them handed the throne on to a son of his own.

Brothers and sisters, do you see now what this list really is? On the surface it is a glorious dynastic record; in fact it is a column of obituaries. Reigned, died; reigned, died. Eight times over. Four different capital cities, which is to say four transfers of power.
Edom had kings, and not one of those kings sat there for long. They had forty "chiefs", and they did not have a single covenant.

And in that very same stretch of time, Jacob's descendants had nothing whatever — no king, no city, no territory. All they had was one sentence: "The land which I gave to Abraham and Isaac, I will give it to you, and to your offspring after you I will give the land."
On the one side, a government you can see. On the other, a promise you cannot. One of them arrives quickly; the other arrives slowly.

And there is one more detail we cannot afford to miss. In verse 39 the last of the kings is Hadad, and his wife is named Mehetabel (מְהֵיטַבְאֵל), which means "God makes good", "God deals graciously." In the entire roll of the kings of Edom, that is the only name that carries the name of God.
Forty chiefs, eight kings, a whole stretch of territory — and one single name that mentions God. That is the medical report on all that prosperity.

And there is one more name that gives the heart a jolt. Verse 12: "Timna was concubine to Eliphaz, Esau's son; and she bore to Eliphaz Amalek." Amalek — the first nation to attack Israel after the exodus, and for centuries afterwards the enemy of the people of God.
A domestic arrangement nobody paid any attention to grew into an enemy for generations. We will come back to this in section 6.
"Chief" forty times and "died" seven times — what are those two numbers telling us?

The first word (אַלּוּף) properly means "the head of a thousand", and it appears more than forty times in this one chapter; and in that roll of kings in verses 31 to 39, every one of them is recorded by the same formula — so-and-so reigned, the name of his city was such-and-such, and then "so-and-so died", seven times over. More striking still, "reigned in his place" is literally "in his stead, in the place where he sat" — eight kings, eight replacements, and not one of them handed the throne on to a son of his own. So on the surface this list is a glorious dynastic record; in fact it is a column of obituaries. Edom had kings, and not one of them sat there for long; it had forty chiefs, and it did not have a single covenant.
Is God mentioned anywhere in the roll of the kings of Edom?

Only once. In verse 39 the last king, Hadad, has a wife named Mehetabel, which means "God makes good", "God deals graciously" — the only name in the whole roll that carries the name of God. Forty chiefs, eight kings, a whole stretch of territory, and one name that mentions God. That is the medical report on all that prosperity. And it is worth every person who is pushing hard at a career or hard at a ministry stopping to think about. If somebody laid out my last ten years as a list of achievements, how many places on it would God be visible? The longer the list, the more urgently that question needs asking — because the busier a person is, the easier it is to edit God off the list altogether.
3. "Before Any King Reigned over the Children of Israel"
Now let us come back to that verse: "These are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom, before any king reigned over the children of Israel" (Genesis 36:31).

That sentence is inserted deliberately by the narrator. He did not have to write it, and he wrote it anyway. And when he wrote it he used a construction with hope built into it — "before any king reigned over the children of Israel" — and the implication is unmistakable: Israel too will one day have a king.
But when is "one day"? Between Jacob and Saul lie four hundred years of slavery in Egypt, forty years in the wilderness, and three hundred years of judges.
Brothers and sisters, this verse is not saying that the wicked prosper first. This verse is saying: the people of God have to learn how to wait.

Asaph, in Psalm 73, is the man who very nearly went down over exactly this. He says, "But as for me, my feet were almost gone. My steps had nearly slipped. For I was envious of the arrogant, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked." He goes on counting it all up, and by the end of the count he cannot keep his own feet under him.
And then he writes the sentence that turns the whole psalm around: "until I entered God's sanctuary, and considered their latter end."

Change the position and the conclusion changes with it. The same roll of the kings of Edom: stand at the foot of the hill and it is somebody else's splendour; stand inside the sanctuary and it is eight funerals.

And please notice that God did not shortchange Esau. In Deuteronomy chapter 2 God says to Israel, "You are to pass through the border of your brothers, the children of Esau, who dwell in Seir … Don't contend with them; for I will not give you any of their land, no, not so much as for the sole of the foot to tread on, because I have given Mount Seir to Esau for a possession."
That land was God's own gift. God looked after the son who was not on the main line. His kindness reaches everybody.
So this chapter is not asking us to envy Edom, and it is not asking us to look down on Edom either. This chapter is asking us to move to a different vantage point and look at time from there.
What arrives quickly is not necessarily grace. And what arrives slowly is not necessarily forgotten.

Here is something I think about often. Esau is the one who got the land first; Jacob is the one who got the promise first. Land you can move into straight away; a promise you have to wait for. Land can be taken off you by somebody else; a promise cannot. What God gave Esau was a piece of ground. What God gave Jacob was himself — "I am God Almighty", "Behold, I am with you."

So if you have seen nothing at all yet, and the only thing in your hand is a single promise, please do not think your hands are empty. The person who is holding God's word in his hand is the one who genuinely has something.
When I see people who pay God no attention doing better than I am, how do I get myself straightened out?

Asaph in Psalm 73 is the man who very nearly went down over exactly this: "For I was envious of the arrogant, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked." He goes on counting it all up, and by the end of the count he cannot keep his own feet under him. And then he writes the sentence that turns it around: "until I entered God's sanctuary, and considered their latter end." Change the position and the conclusion changes with it. The same roll of the kings of Edom: from the foot of the hill it is somebody else's splendour; from inside the sanctuary it is eight funerals. So in practice the remedy is not to talk yourself out of envying. It is to move to a different position and look from there — deliberately pull your eyes out to what that thing will look like ten years from now, thirty years from now, in eternity.
Did God shortchange this branch, Esau's line?

No. In Deuteronomy chapter 2 God says to Israel, "You are to pass through the border of your brothers, the children of Esau, who dwell in Seir … Don't contend with them; for I will not give you any of their land, no, not so much as for the sole of the foot to tread on, because I have given Mount Seir to Esau for a possession." That land was God's own gift. So this chapter is not asking us to envy Edom, and it is not asking us to look down on Edom. God's kindness reaches everybody. What has to be seen clearly is that the two gifts are not the same thing: what God gave Esau was a piece of ground; what God gave Jacob was himself — "I am God Almighty", "Behold, I am with you." Ground can be taken away. The promise cannot.
4. One Settles Down, One Looks Up

The last sentence of this chapter is, "This is Esau, the father of the Edomites." And then the camera swings round, and Genesis 37:1 says, "Jacob lived in the land of his father's travels, in the land of Canaan."
Please read those two verses side by side.

The Edomites are set out "according to their families, after their places, and by their names" — a complete administrative file; and they are "in the land of their possession", where they have their "habitations." The words underneath are אֲחֻזָּה (a holding, a possession) and מוֹשָׁב (a dwelling place), and both of them belong to the vocabulary of settling down.

And Jacob? He "travels" — גּוּר, to sojourn as a resident alien. That is the shared status of all three generations: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. They lived on the land of the promise, and all their lives long they were strangers on it.

Hebrews chapter 11 explains it with great clarity: "These all died in faith … having confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth … But now they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed of them, to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them."
One settles down; the other looks up.

Brothers and sisters, I am not saying a Christian ought not to own a house, ought not to have a career, ought not to make a good life of his days. I am saying this: has your heart settled down on this earth too early?
To settle down means: I have arrived, this is what I wanted, and from here on all I have to do is maintain it. To look up means: this is good, and I know that this is not the destination.
The Edomites had an address; the Israelites had a promise. Four thousand years later, Edom is gone, and the people of God are still here.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot
There are several holes that are very easy to step into when you preach this chapter.

The first distortion is to skip the genealogy and not preach it at all. Those forty-three verses of names were written deliberately: even the branch that was set aside, God accounts for down to the last detail. Skip it, and the congregation never learns how much weight God gives to every single person. The test is this: when the congregation has heard you, do they come away thinking this chapter was of no use, or have they seen the heart of God?

The second distortion is to take "Edom is the enemy" and reason from it to some group of people alive today. Edom did indeed become hostile to Israel later on, but that is historical narrative, not an ethnic label, and it certainly cannot be used to put a brand on any modern ethnic group, nation or community. Any use of this chapter to justify contempt, exclusion or hatred we must refuse on the spot.

The third distortion is to preach "Edom had kings first" as though the wicked win in the end. Psalm 73 has already given the answer: you have to enter the sanctuary and consider their latter end. Preach only the first half and the congregation will stumble. The test is very simple: when this sermon is over, the picture left behind in the congregation's mind — is it the kings of Edom, or the King of kings?

The fourth distortion is to preach "God looked after Esau" as though it makes no difference how a person lives. God gave Esau Mount Seir; that is his common kindness. What God gave Jacob was the covenant. Kindness reaches all people; the covenant is a thing set apart. Blur the two together and the gospel goes out of focus.

The fifth distortion is to use this chapter to comfort people with "whatever you are behind in now, you are bound to win it all back in the end." That is still ranking; it has merely pushed the day of reckoning further back. What this chapter is meant to dismantle is not your ranking. It is the business of comparing itself.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: our culture lives inside lists. From the ranking of marks at school, to whose child got into which university, to who in the class group chat has changed his car, who has emigrated, whose child is getting married. We are not necessarily unkind people, but it is very hard for us not to compare. That Edomite list in chapter 36 is exactly that group-chat message, four thousand years earlier. Brothers and sisters, here is what comparing actually is: taking the ranking of this moment and using it to measure a thing God is calculating in eternity. You would not use a stopwatch to measure how tall a tree has grown. This week, if there is a list, a number or a page that you look at every single day, try switching it off for one week and see what happens.

The second question: we very often overlook what a small thing can grow into. Timna, a concubine nobody paid any attention to; the son she bore, Amalek, became the enemy of God's people for centuries. There are matters like that in our own homes too — a sentence that was never dealt with, a relative never reconciled with, a sum of money that was never properly settled. We say: it is a small thing, let it go. But small things have sons, and the sons grow up. That sentence about Reuben in the last chapter was not settled until chapter 49; that sentence about Timna in this chapter was not settled until Exodus. This week, go and deal with the small thing you keep saying is "nothing."
Was the place where Esau really went off course that bowl of red stew?

Most people assume it was; in fact the text points at something else. Verse 2 says the wives he took were "from the daughters of Canaan"; chapter 26 puts it very bluntly — "They grieved Isaac's and Rebekah's spirits" — and in chapter 28 Isaac gives Jacob the particular charge, "You shall not take a wife of the daughters of Canaan." And verse 12 gives the heart a real jolt: Eliphaz's concubine Timna bore Amalek — the first nation to attack Israel after the exodus. A domestic arrangement nobody paid any attention to grew into an enemy for generations. So the place where a person really goes off course is very often not one impulsive decision. It is his choice of the people he will live his days alongside.
7. Living 321 Out — Handing the Ranking Back to God
Brothers and sisters, let us tie this lesson back into the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model. God looked after Esau, and even commanded Israel not to contend with him for his land. The Lord Jesus said, "For he makes his sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the just and the unjust." My role model is this: his kindness reaches everybody, and not only his own people. So I cannot receive grace with one hand and hope with the other that somebody else comes to grief.

The Bible is my standard. My feelings say, "This is not fair"; the standard says, "until I entered God's sanctuary, and considered their latter end." Feelings measure today; the standard measures eternity. When the two of them collide, listen to the standard.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. Comparison is the thing that ferments in the heart most easily of all; the more you rely on your intellect to work it out, the more troubled you become, and the more you count it up, the more aggrieved you feel. Rely on the heart and lean on the Holy Spirit, and gladness comes back: carry that sense of grievance into prayer, and let the Holy Spirit change your position rather than change your ranking.

Let Jesus be King. The kings of Edom came one after another, and all of it was coup and turnover; Israel's king had to wait until God said the time had come. Letting Jesus be King means not reaching out your own hand to snatch that seat — whether it is the seat at home, the seat in the church, or that seat inside you marked "I have to win."

Let Jesus receive all the glory. In the whole roll of the kings of Edom only one name carries the name of God. If the list of our life's achievements likewise has only one or two items on it that have anything to do with God, then however long that list may be, it is empty. Give thanks in everything and hand the glory back to him — that is how a thing gets counted into eternity.

Establish God's system. The Edomites are settled "in the land of their possession"; Jacob "lived in the land of his father's travels." One settles down; the other looks up. To establish God's system is to keep the heart pointed the whole time at that city with foundations; we do put up houses on this earth, but we know what it is we are really building.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One and the Same List
We come to this list carrying four kinds of heart.

The proud heart says, "Well, at least I am not like them." Be careful — that is the Pharisee's prayer in the temple. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights: sitting down in the examiner's seat and marking other people's papers on God's behalf. Humility is returning to the position proper to a human being and admitting that I need grace exactly as much as they do; I simply received mercy first.

The fearful heart says, "Am I going to be left behind?" You watch other people move ahead one after another, and you are afraid the age will throw you away. Brothers and sisters, all eight of those kings have the same sentence written at the end of them: he died. The queue you are so afraid of dropping out of is, every last person in it, walking towards the same finishing line.

The ashamed heart says, "My whole life long, I am probably just the one who pastures the donkeys." Then listen very carefully to verse 24: the boy pasturing the donkeys got written into the Bible. God records names, not job titles. That one spring of water you found out in the wilderness — he saw it.

The wounded heart says, "Why is it they have it and I do not?" That is a real question, and Psalm 73 is one whole psalm written about it. God did not rebuke Asaph for asking it. What God did was bring him into the sanctuary. You may bring that question with you — only remember to carry it into the sanctuary, and not sit down at the foot of the hill and do the sums by yourself.
Four kinds of heart, one and the same list. Change the position, and that list changes its meaning.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do

First, towards God. Take the thing that most aggrieves you and carry it into God's presence, and ask him one question: "Lord, what does this amount to in eternity?" Then be still, and listen to what he says.

Second, towards yourself. Write down the one thing you compare most often — income, children, the fruitfulness of your service, other people's praise. Write it down, and then lay it down before God for a week.

Third, towards other people. Pray a concrete blessing over one person you have envied, or over one person something in you still refuses to concede to. Name him, say out loud the good he has received, and genuinely ask God to give him twice as much.

Fourth, towards daily living. This week, switch off that number or that list that makes you compare — that page, that group chat, that leaderboard. Stop it for one week, and see whether your heart grows quiet.
Fifth, towards your calling. Check whether your heart has settled down on this earth too early. Ask yourself one question: if God told me tomorrow to strike camp, could I still pull up the pegs?

Sixth, tell it to one friend outside the church, in three sentences. First: there is a whole chapter in the Bible recording a family who prospered earlier than the people of God did. Second: in that list, every single king's entry ends with the words "he died." Third: so I have learned not to use a ranking to measure a thing God is counting in eternity.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that I will no longer use somebody else's timetable to measure the work God is doing in me.
I declare that I will not snatch at that seat; let Jesus be King, and when the time comes he will surely bring it to pass.
I declare that I will bless the people I have envied and the people something in me has refused to concede to.
I declare that my heart will not settle down on this earth; I desire that city with foundations.
All I have in my hand is a single promise and nothing to show for it — how do I hold on this week?

Start by putting it a different way: the person who is holding God's word in his hand is the one who genuinely has something. In practical terms there are three things you can do. First, write that promise down and stick it somewhere you will see it, and read it aloud once a day — not to hypnotise yourself, but so that it comes in front of your eyes more often than the comparisons on social media do. Second, keep a record of small things: like that boy pasturing donkeys who came upon the hot springs, write down every day one small thing God did that day. Third, find a companion, and once a week ask each other, "Are you still holding on to that word?" Waiting with nobody alongside you turns very easily into loneliness; it is waiting with someone alongside you that lasts.

Forty-three verses of names, forty chiefs, eight kings, four capital cities, a whole stretch of territory you can point to on a map. And then the camera swings round: "Jacob lived in the land of his father's travels, in the land of Canaan."

Seen through human eyes, this chapter is a contrast: that side has everything already, this side has nothing yet. Seen through God's eyes, this chapter is also a contrast: on that side it is written eight times over, "he died"; on this side there is one sentence that has never changed — "I will give it to you, and to your offspring after you."

So the focus is on Jesus, not on myself, not on other people, not on my circumstances. Not I, but Christ. I do not have to compare, because my worth is not located inside a ranking; I do not have to hurry, because the One who promised has never once been late; I do not have to be afraid of being left behind, because the One who ran the whole course on my behalf is already seated on the throne. Edom produced eight kings, and every one of them died; and the King who came out of Jacob's line is the One who died and rose again, and of his kingdom there will be no end.

May God bless every one of us this week: to walk up from the foot of the hill into the sanctuary, and from that position to look once more at the list that has been aggrieving us. May the comparing in our hearts be taken away; may we be willing to live as strangers on this earth, with our eyes on that city with foundations, waiting for the King of kings. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point of the lesson into the head, the second carries it from the head into the heart, the third carries it from the heart into the week. If there is not enough time, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third transformation — without reaching the third, this lesson stops at the level of mindset and goes no further.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear mindset.
1. ★★★ From the foot of the hill it is somebody else's splendour; from inside the sanctuary it is eight funerals. Why does changing the position change the conclusion?
2. ★★ God gave Esau a piece of ground, and gave Jacob himself. Where does the difference between those two things lie?
3. ★ A boy pasturing donkeys came upon the hot springs, and even that got written into the Bible. What does that say to someone who serves quietly?
4. ★★ Forty chiefs, eight kings, and only one name that mentions God. On your own list of the last ten years, in how many places can God be seen?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (they will collapse sooner or later), fearful (am I going to be behind for the rest of my life?), ashamed (I still have nothing to show for it), wounded (nobody remembers anything I have done). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Please read aloud: "I am God Almighty … Behold, I am with you." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ Whose results do you most often use to measure yourself by? And where does that comparison take place — the class group chat, social media, the family gathering?
8. ★ Finish it in one sentence: "The one promise I am holding on to right now is …"
9. ★★ This week, where are you going to put that promise up, and when will you read it? Please say it very concretely.

Leader's reminder: question nine will touch a long-standing sense of falling behind and the hurt of not being seen. Do not brush it aside with "when God's time comes you will have it." If someone speaks of years of waiting and disappointment, stay with him privately after the meeting.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ In your own home, who is the one "nobody remembers what he did"? How are you going to remember him once this week?
11. ★ The same question in another setting: in your church or your workplace, which piece of unseen service ought to be said out loud?
12. ★★★ The practice of changing position: this week, every time something aggrieves you, ask first, "What will this look like ten years from now?" Say which situation aggrieves you most often.
13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — and every day this week send each other one "small thing God did today." Say his name now, in front of the group.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First: there is a whole chapter of the Bible that is a list, recording forty chiefs and eight kings of one family. Second: read it carefully and every one of those eight kings has "he died" written after him, while the other branch had nothing at all, only a promise. Third: so what I learned is that what arrives quickly is not necessarily grace, and what arrives slowly is not necessarily forgotten. Write down now who you are going to tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: the one promise you are holding in your hand, and the person nobody remembers whom you are going to remember this week. Then pray for each other, asking the Lord to lift our eyes off other people's lists and bring them back to himself.
